Reviewed the Jenkins CI added on `agent_tools` relative to PR #1132’s base (`c6be0d59..c36c8717`). The cluster and client scripts pass static shell checks; the Lua regression checker also parses successfully. I did not run Jenkins or Slurm jobs because that requires the real controllers and allocations.

The main merge blocker is the team-workstation configuration.

- `personal`, `stellar_cpu`, and `perlmutter_gpu` are correctly designed: their setup docs require a regular Pipeline sourced from `*/main`, then the trusted pipeline separately checks out the candidate PR. Their GitHub token is scoped to the API calls, not candidate build commands.
- `team_workstation` is not safe in the same way. Its documented Multibranch Pipeline executes `ci/jenkins/jenkinsfile.team_workstation` from each PR revision, and line 31 then loads `jenkinsfile.personal` from that same candidate checkout. The comment that it is “trusted main” is true only for explicit CLI builds sent to the `main` child—not automatic PR builds. Native multibranch pipelines deliberately execute branch-specific Jenkinsfiles. [Jenkins multibranch documentation](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/pipeline/multibranch/) also warns that SCM credentials can be exposed to users able to modify those Jenkinsfiles. [Jenkins security guidance](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/security/securing-org-folders-and-multibranch-pipelines/)

Before merging, I recommend either:

1. Remove/disable automatic PR execution from the team workstation and use the existing main-pinned parameterized-job model; or
2. Replace the native multibranch definition with a centrally configured trusted Pipeline mechanism, then have that pipeline perform the explicitly controlled candidate checkout.

Do not rely on an in-repository `load` to make a multibranch PR trusted—it remains candidate-controlled.

Two further cleanup recommendations:

- The legacy generic [`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`](/Users/mfrancis/Documents/gkeyll/code/gkeyll_v0/gkeyll/ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile:13) appears intended for multibranch use (`CHANGE_ID`, `checkout scm`) but is undocumented and therefore also candidate-sourced if configured as a normal multibranch job. Either remove it in favor of the supported jobs, or redesign it as a main-pinned parameterized pipeline. Also remove its `printenv` at line 15; CI logs should not dump all ambient environment variables.
- If the team workstation will execute PRs from arbitrary GitHub authors, run its build agent under a dedicated low-privilege account or disposable VM/container, with no SSH keys, persistent personal data, Jenkins home access, or nonessential credentials. Main-pinning protects the pipeline authority, but compiling a PR necessarily executes arbitrary candidate code.

Everything else I inspected was broadly well thought out: selector validation, shallow explicit checkouts, status-token scoping, Slurm cancellation/accounting, artifact collection, and separate candidate/baseline builds are all solid.

I removed the legacy ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile.

Regarding the team workstation, I need to clarify how it works. Is jenkinsfile.team_workstation essentially wrapping jenkinsfile.personal, so that it runs jenkinsfile.team_workstation from main which calls its jenkinsfile.personal, and separately runs jenkinsfile.team_worstation from the candidate PR which then runs its jenkinsfile.personal?

Yes—with one crucial qualification.

A native Multibranch Pipeline creates a separate child job per SCM revision:

- `.../main`: Jenkins retrieves `jenkinsfile.team_workstation` from `main`, which loads `jenkinsfile.personal` from the `main` checkout. This is trusted.
- `.../PR-123`: Jenkins retrieves `jenkinsfile.team_workstation` from the PR’s candidate revision, which then loads `jenkinsfile.personal` from that same PR checkout. This is not trusted.

So the wrapper does not cause the PR child to use the `main` version. Jenkins selects and loads the configured script path from the child job’s SCM revision before any wrapper code can run.

The CLI intentionally targets the `main` child, so its manually requested builds use the trusted `main` wrapper and personal pipeline. But the two-minute multibranch scan creates/runs PR child jobs whose pipeline code is candidate-controlled.

Yes. The key is to move pipeline authority out of the PR child’s SCM revision while still allowing the trusted workflow to fetch and test that revision. I’ll check the currently supported Jenkins mechanisms so the tradeoffs are concrete.

content.text:
Yes—there are two good designs, depending on whether automatic PR CI is important.

1. Main-pinned regular Pipeline — simplest and safest

Configure one ordinary Jenkins Pipeline job from `*/main`, using the current `jenkinsfile.personal` logic adapted for the team environment. It receives `CANDIDATE_PR`/reference parameters, then performs its explicit candidate checkout.

The team launcher could continue to submit selected runs to this job. Automatic checks could be omitted initially, or added later through a small trusted GitHub polling/webhook component that submits parameters to that one job.

Pros:

- No PR can alter the Pipeline Groovy code.
- Uses only ordinary Jenkins functionality already needed for the personal/cluster jobs.
- Much easier to reason about and maintain.
- The existing personal implementation is already close to what is needed.

Cons:

- You lose native multibranch per-PR child jobs and automatic discovery.
- Automatic PR triggering requires trusted glue—webhook/poller/API logic—to turn a PR event into a parameterized build.
- A single job normally serializes builds, so several active PRs queue rather than run concurrently.

2. Retain multibranch discovery, but use a centralized trusted pipeline — best if automatic PR CI is required

Jenkins supports a “central pipeline” approach using a plugin such as [Multibranch Pipeline Inline Definition](https://plugins.jenkins.io/inline-pipeline). Jenkins itself explicitly identifies centralized Pipeline plugins as the remedy for SCM-credential exposure in multibranch jobs. [Security guidance](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/security/securing-org-folders-and-multibranch-pipelines/)

The multibranch job would still discover `main` and PRs, create `PR-123` child jobs, and trigger on scans/webhooks. But every child would execute a Pipeline defined in Jenkins configuration or in a trusted global shared library—not either file from the PR.

The centralized pipeline should contain the current trusted logic:

- Read `CHANGE_ID` and `CHANGE_TARGET`.
- Reject non-`main` PR targets.
- Fetch the PR head explicitly.
- Build/test the candidate.
- Fetch/build the baseline separately.
- Bind the GitHub credential only for checkout/API-status operations, never around candidate-controlled commands.

Do not use `load 'ci/jenkins/jenkinsfile.personal'` in that central pipeline: after checkout, `load` would again read the candidate’s copy. Put that logic in the Jenkins-managed definition or a trusted shared library pinned to a reviewed version.

Pros:

- Preserves automatic PR discovery, webhook/periodic scans, per-PR history, and distinct Jenkins child jobs.
- Keeps pipeline authority out of candidate code.
- Closest behaviorally to the current team-workstation design.

Cons:

- Adds a Jenkins plugin and central configuration that must be backed up, reviewed, and updated deliberately.
- The inline-definition plugin currently requires Jenkins 2.479.3 or newer; check the controller version before choosing it. [Plugin details](https://plugins.jenkins.io/inline-pipeline)
- More setup complexity than a single main-pinned job.

My recommendation: use option 1 unless automatic CI for every PR is an immediate requirement. If it is, use option 2; it preserves the existing workflow without accepting PR-provided Pipeline code.

In either case, candidate builds still execute arbitrary candidate C/Makefile/shell code. The team build agent should remain isolated and low-privilege; trusted pipeline source protects Jenkins authority and credentials, not the machine from code being tested.
Automatic CI for every PR into main is a requirement.

That rules out the simple regular-job-only design. The team workstation should retain multibranch PR discovery but replace PR-sourced pipeline code with a centralized trusted definition; Jenkins documents that exact pattern for this threat model. The remaining decision is where the trusted definition lives.

content.text:
“Inline” means the Pipeline Groovy script is stored in Jenkins job configuration, rather than being read from a `Jenkinsfile` in the branch or PR.

For this case, the Multibranch Pipeline Inline Definition plugin adds a multibranch mode like “Common pipeline definition for markerfile.” Jenkins still scans GitHub and creates `main` and `PR-123` child jobs, but every child runs the same centrally configured script. The PR only supplies the source code that the trusted script explicitly checks out and tests.

A minimal inline definition could be conceptually:

```groovy
@Library('gkeyll-ci@main') _
runGkeyllTeamCi()
```

Here:

- The one-line script lives in Jenkins configuration.
- `gkeyll-ci` is a Jenkins “Global Trusted Pipeline Library.”
- Jenkins config pins that library to reviewed `main` and disallows a PR from selecting another version.
- `runGkeyllTeamCi()` contains the current team/personal workflow: inspect `CHANGE_ID`, fetch the PR head, build it, fetch its `main` baseline, run tests, and post status.
- It must never `load` a file from the candidate checkout.

The practical benefit of the shared library is reviewability and version control: the substantial Groovy workflow stays in a repository instead of a large Jenkins UI text field. The library repository could be this Gkeyll repository, but I would put its trusted CI implementation in a location not fetched from the candidate checkout and configure Jenkins to retrieve only `main`.

The alternative “full inline Jenkinsfile” means pasting the entire several-hundred-line workflow into Jenkins configuration. It works, but updates are harder to review, audit, and reproduce.

Since automatic PR CI is required, I recommend the inline-definition + trusted shared-library design. It preserves per-PR multibranch jobs and automatic triggering, while ensuring that the PR cannot replace the logic that controls credentials, checkouts, or status reporting.

What if in the future we do want to change the Jenkins CI, e.g. add valgrind checks as part of it? How could a subsequent PR change the Jenkins CI if the proposed workflow is meant to work only with the library stored in main?

A normal PR could change the CI library’s source, but production PR jobs would intentionally continue running the currently trusted `main` version until that PR is merged. That is the tradeoff that prevents a PR from granting itself new Jenkins authority.

The safe update workflow is:

1. Open a PR that changes the trusted CI library—for example, add a `Valgrind` stage.
2. Review it as infrastructure/security-sensitive code.
3. Validate it with a separate staging Jenkins job that an administrator explicitly configures to use that reviewed PR branch or commit. This is a deliberate administrative action, not something the PR can request for itself.
4. Merge the PR.
5. The production shared library advances to `main`; subsequent automatic PR builds run the new Valgrind stage.

For low-risk changes, step 3 can simply be a manual “run the staging CI job against this exact commit.” For a mature setup, maintain:

- Production multibranch CI → trusted shared library pinned to `main`.
- Staging multibranch/parameterized CI → same library, but an administrator can temporarily select a reviewed CI-change commit.
- Optional library tests/linting → run on every CI-library PR without needing privileged Jenkins credentials.

This is similar to changing GitHub Actions workflows protected by branch rules: the new workflow becomes authoritative only after review and merge. It does mean CI-infrastructure changes do not fully self-test on the production controller before merge—but that is precisely the security boundary.

What exactly is the .gkeyll-team-ci file for? are there alternative approaches?

`.gkeyll-team-ci` is only a discovery marker for the Multibranch Pipeline Inline Definition plugin. Its contents are never executed.

The plugin needs one repository file whose presence says, “create a child job for this branch/PR.” We configured it to use that marker, then Jenkins runs its controller-owned bootstrap—not a file from the PR.

Without a marker, that plugin cannot decide which repository revisions should receive jobs. The marker does not establish trust; the bootstrap’s explicit checkout of trusted `main` does.

Alternatives:

- Use an existing always-present file, such as `README.md` or `Makefile`, as the marker. This avoids the new file but is less self-explanatory. A PR can still remove it.
- Use a different centralized-pipeline plugin, such as “Pipeline: Multibranch with defaults,” which provides a default Pipeline model. It is an alternative but is less current/commonly deployed than Inline Definition.
- Use a regular main-pinned Pipeline triggered by a webhook/polling service. This needs no marker, but you would need custom trusted automation to discover PRs and submit parameterized builds.
- Use a trusted Jenkins shared library with the inline-definition plugin. This improves code organization but still needs the plugin’s marker.

For the present design, I prefer the dedicated marker: its purpose is obvious and isolated. Once the workstation becomes a merge gate, requiring its GitHub status prevents a PR from bypassing CI by deleting the marker.
But couldn't a PR also delete .gkeyll-team-ci?

Yes. A PR can delete or rename `.gkeyll-team-ci`; then the inline-definition plugin may not create/build that PR child job.

That does not let the PR execute untrusted Pipeline code, but it can suppress its CI run. While CI is infrastructure-only, that is acceptable operationally. Once CI becomes a merge gate, configure GitHub branch protection to require the team status; a PR with no resulting status cannot merge.

If you want to avoid that behavior even before branch protection, use an existing file that every normal Gkeyll PR necessarily retains, such as `Makefile`, as the marker. It is still technically deletable, but deleting it would make the candidate impossible to build and obvious in review. The dedicated marker is clearer; the existing-file marker is slightly more resistant to accidental removal.
could this marker file live in ci/jenkins?

Yes. For example, use:

```text
ci/jenkins/.team-workstation-marker
```

Then configure the inline-definition plugin’s marker path to that exact path.

That keeps CI-only plumbing together and makes its purpose clearer. A PR could still delete it, so the same future branch-protection recommendation applies.

Aligned the team README’s hierarchy with the personal README:

- Installation → Install Jenkins / Open Jenkins browser / Set up Jenkins
- Matching setup subsections
- Launching CI jobs → CLI launch / Browser launch
- Troubleshooting → Jenkins API and builds / Numerical regression differences

The team-specific centralized multibranch setup and trusted-workflow-change procedure now live within those matching sections. `git diff --check` passes.
Why did you change ci/jenkins/jenkinsfile.personal?

I changed it for two team-workstation requirements:

1. The Jenkins inline bootstrap already allocates the team agent before it loads the trusted workflow. `jenkinsfile.personal` previously always called `node(label)` itself, which would create a nested agent request and can deadlock a one-executor workstation. I wrapped its body in `runCi`; personal CI still calls it inside `node(label)`, while team CI sets `CI_NODE_ALREADY_ALLOCATED=true` and reuses the bootstrap’s allocation.

2. Team builds need to archive the commit of the trusted CI workflow that was loaded from `main` (or a staging ref). The personal workflow now writes and archives `ci-trusted-ci-commit.txt` only when the bootstrap supplies `CI_TRUSTED_CI_COMMIT`.

For ordinary personal CI, neither environment variable is set, so its runtime behavior is unchanged.
